value: MoreSteam's control plan is the central record of every significant process characteristic; for each one it names the chart used and, as chart champion, the process owner.
reason: The old explanation drew on MoreSteam's stakeholder template, which the card does not cite and which goes beyond where the control plan names the process owner. Control Plan: 'The control plan is the centralized document to keep track of the status of all significant process characteristics'; 'Chart Champion: Name of the process owner.'

value: In a lean project, how does the sponsor's role differ from the implementation team leader's, according to the Starter Kit?
reason: The Starter Kit describes two roles, 'Implementation Team Leader' (p. 39) and 'Team Leader' (p. 41). The contrast with the sponsor on p. 40 is with the implementation team leader: 'While the implementation team leader focuses on keeping the project team on track with its assignments, the sponsor's role is to push the team…'.

value: The implementation team leader keeps the team on track with its assignments; the sponsor pushes it to reach its overall objectives and removes barriers.
reason: Names the role the source actually contrasts with the sponsor (PDF p. 40), so the card does not clash with the facilitator card's 'team leader', a different role.

value: The two work closely after an event: the implementation team leader runs the follow-up, while the sponsor, ideally the director of the division concerned, holds the team to its goals.
reason: Explains why the roles differ. PDF pp. 39–40: the implementation team leader organises follow-up check-ins; 'Ideally, the sponsor is a director or leader of a division within which the Lean project is taking place'; the sponsor 'will work closely with the implementation team leader following any Lean event'.

value: Like the seal and panel fit a carmaker specifies so that a door shuts with the solid sound buyers expect.
reason: An oven temperature is a process setting, not 'an element of a design or a characteristic of a part', so the old example could teach that process inputs are CTQs. LeanOhio p. 4 gives the car-door case: 'Car door sound when closing might be a CTC, while the dimensional tolerances and cushioning that produce those conditions are CTQ's'.

value: A feature of a design, or of a part, that the customer regards as essential to its quality.
reason: Tier C, facts only in our own words (CONTENT-POLICY.md §3, tier C); the old back repeated 18 of LeanOhio's 20 words ('An element of a design or a characteristic of a part that is essential to quality in the eyes of the customer', p. 4).

value: According to LeanOhio's glossary, what training and projects make up the path to Black Belt?
reason: This is a subject deck; 'the route to becoming a certified Black Belt' frames LeanOhio as a certifier. The glossary (p. 2) defines a Black Belt as one 'certified following a four-month training and application program and successful completion of two Six Sigma Projects'; the back is unchanged.

value: A problem-solving framework for continual improvement, which the Starter Kit credits to W. Edwards Deming; it is also called Plan-Do-Study-Act.
reason: The origin of the cycle is not settled outside this source, so the attribution is given as the kit's own. Starter Kit PDF p. 11: 'originally conceived by Dr. W. Edwards Deming'.

value: It is a tool for managing rather than only reporting: the management team uses it to steer how a strategy or day-to-day operations are put into practice.
reason: The old 'not only at recording results' was the card's own inference presented as the source's. Wikipedia lead: 'a performance management report used by a management team, and typically focused on managing the implementation of a strategy or operational activities'. Now framed as why it is called a management report.

value: These roles lead the planning and running of the project; the kit's role descriptions also cover team members and the implementation team leader.
reason: 'These are the roles the Starter Kit describes' overstated: its role descriptions (PDF pp. 39–41) also include 'Team Member' and 'Implementation Team Leader'.

value: Anyone the project affects, or who can sway it, without taking part in the project work themselves.
reason: Tier C, own words only (CONTENT-POLICY.md §3, tier C); the old back repeated a 12-word run of LeanOhio's 'People who will be affected by the project or can influence it but who are not directly involved with doing the project work' (p. 13).

value: In event-based projects, the kit has the team leader help the facilitator prepare the ground so that the event is productive.
reason: Tier C, own words only; the old text repeated a 14-word run of 'the team leader assists the facilitator in setting the stage for a productive event' (PDF p. 41).

value: The template treats the dates as provisional: the team fixes them during the project, according to what it will need later.
reason: Tier C, own words only; the old text repeated a 13-word run of 'These dates will be confirmed with the team during the project in the context of future needs' (PDF p. 115).

value: MoreSteam's rule of thumb: choose DMAIC for improving a process that already exists, and PDCA for a change too small to justify a full DMAIC project.
reason: Tier C, own words only; the old text repeated an 11-word run of MoreSteam's 'PDCA when the change is small enough not to need a full DMAIC project'.

value: MoreSteam warns that, without the routine of daily management, even a well-planned strategic initiative tends to move in fits and starts and then stop.
reason: Tier C, own words only; the old text repeated an 11-word run of 'even well-designed strategic initiatives tend to advance in bursts and stall'.
